rmt-2015-calc-02.title: Differentiate
rmt-2015-calc-02.body:
Contestant $n$ has speed $\frac{n t^{n-1}}{2}$, which at $t=2$ is $n2^{n-2}$: $\frac12,2,6,16,40$. The sum is $\frac{129}2$ and the average over 5 contestants is $\frac{129}{10}=12.9$.

**Answer: $12.9$ mph**

rmt-2015-calc-03.title: Cheaper paint at each point
rmt-2015-calc-03.body:
Green is cheaper when $x^2\le2x$, i.e. $0\le x\le2$; red is cheaper on $[2,5]$. The minimum cost is $\int_0^2x^2\,dx+\int_2^52x\,dx=\frac83+(25-4)=\frac{71}3$.

**Answer: $\frac{71}{3}$ dollars**

rmt-2015-calc-04.title: Implicit differentiation
rmt-2015-calc-04.body:
The roots have product $-7$ and sum $-u$, so the other root is $-\frac7y$ and $y-\frac7y=-u$. Differentiating with respect to time: $\left(1+\frac7{y^2}\right)y'=-u'=-2$. At $y=4$: $y'=\frac{-2}{1+\frac7{16}}=-\frac{32}{23}$.

**Answer: $-\frac{32}{23}$**

rmt-2015-calc-05.title: Taylor expansions
rmt-2015-calc-05.body:
Near $0$: $\sin x^\alpha\approx x^\alpha$ and $\cos x^\beta-1\approx-\frac{x^{2\beta}}2$. The ratio behaves like $-2x^{\alpha-2\beta}$. For the limit to exist and be nonzero we need $\alpha=2\beta$, and then the limit is $-2$.

**Answer: $-2$**

rmt-2015-calc-06.title: Product rule
rmt-2015-calc-06.body:
By the product rule the derivative at $0$ is $\sum_{k=1}^{16}\prod_{n\ne k}\frac1n=\sum_{k=1}^{16}\frac{k}{16!}=\frac{136}{16!}=\frac{17}{2\cdot15!}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{17}{2\cdot15!}$**

rmt-2015-calc-07.title: Split into circle areas
rmt-2015-calc-07.body:
The integrand equals $\sqrt{2-x}\left(\sqrt x+\sqrt{x+2}\right)=\sqrt{2x-x^2}+\sqrt{4-x^2}$. The first term integrates to the area under the upper half of the circle $(x-1)^2+y^2=1$: $\frac\pi2$. The second gives a quarter of the disk of radius 2: $\pi$. Sum: $\frac{3\pi}2$.

**Answer: $\frac{3\pi}{2}$**

rmt-2015-calc-08.title: Substitution
rmt-2015-calc-08.body:
Let $y=2+x$: $\int_2^\infty\frac{(y-1)^{2013}}{y^{2015}}dy=\int_2^\infty\frac1{y^2}\left(1-\frac1y\right)^{2013}dy$. With $u=1-\frac1y$, $du=\frac{dy}{y^2}$, the integral is $\int_{1/2}^1u^{2013}du=\frac1{2014}\left(1-2^{-2014}\right)$. Multiplying by $2014$ gives $1-2^{-2014}$.

**Answer: $1-2^{-2014}$**

rmt-2015-calc-09.title: Probabilistic view
rmt-2015-calc-09.body:
The product is the expected value of $5^X3^{1-X}$ where $X$ is uniform on $[0,1]$ (choose each binary digit of $X$ with probability $\frac12$). That is $\int_0^13\left(\frac53\right)^xdx=\frac{3\left(\frac53-1\right)}{\ln(5/3)}=\frac2{\ln(5/3)}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac2{\ln(5/3)}$**

rmt-2015-calc-10.title: Conserved quantity
rmt-2015-calc-10.body:
Multiply by $u'$ and integrate: $K=\frac{(u')^2}2-\frac{u^3}3+\frac{u^6}6$ is constant. At $x=0$: $K=\frac{49}2-\frac83+\frac{64}6=\frac{65}2$. So $(u')^2=65+\frac23u^3-\frac13u^6$. Maxima of $|u'|$ occur where $u''=0$, i.e. $u^2=u^5$, so $u=0$ or $u=1$. At $u=1$: $(u')^2=65+\frac23-\frac13=\frac{196}3$, larger than $65$ at $u=0$. The solution does pass through $u=1$ (the energy curve is a closed curve in the $(u,u')$ phase plane which the solution traverses completely). Hence the maximum is $\sqrt{\frac{196}3}=\frac{14\sqrt3}3$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{14\sqrt3}{3}$**
